All cell systems / types (GSM, CDMA, etc) track the locations of ALL cell phones that are on their
network. This is part of how the systems work, it's what enables you to walk / drive around and stay
connected (most of the time) to your system. While the location accuracy may not be down to within
the square foot of where you are, this information is required to regulate the power that your phone is
outputting so it can make reliable connection to the cell you are in, and so that the cell you may be
transitioning into will be ready to acquire your signal seamlessly without dropping you (most of the
time) from your connection/conversation.
This is more basic than using a built in GPS receiver, which a lot of phones have these days also.
Yes, the fact that apps also do this, and then forward that data to the apps database, is what gets
folks panties in a twist. As it should, especially if the app does not give you the option to turn this
telemetry data off.
I'm not a lawyer, just a comms guy, but it seems to me that if you are using an app that reports this
stuff back (Google maps, iMaps, most of the weather apps, etc), they make it clear in their
information on the app that this takes place, makes it clear that it can or can not be turned off (and
how to turn it off), and someone still uses it regardless, then it's on the consumer to find the apps
they are willing to use.
